questions.stem: The stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of:

options.explanation: Those are not distances.
This is the sum law of record.
Those are factors, not the two distances.
Only one braking leg exists.

questions.stem: Thinking distance is the distance travelled while the driver:

options.text: Applies the brakes at maximum force
options.explanation: That is the braking leg.
No acceleration happens in an emergency stop.
Gear changes play no part.

options.text: Reacts to the emergency and prepares to stop
options.explanation: The reaction window is exactly what the thinking distance covers.

questions.stem: The average human reaction time of record is:

options.explanation: Far shorter than the quoted figure.
Far longer than the quoted figure.
About a quarter of a second.
Ten times too long.

questions.stem: Which condition lengthens a driver's reaction time?

options.text: Tiredness, phone distraction, alcohol or drugs
options.explanation: All four raise the reaction time, stretching the thinking distance.
Those do not lengthen the reaction.
Engine noise is not the listed driver.
Lighting is not a reaction-time factor of record.

questions.stem: The braking distance is the distance covered:

options.explanation: That is the thinking leg.

options.text: Under the braking force, in metres
options.explanation: The braking leg's definition of record.
No distance is covered after stopping.
An emergency stop decelerates.

questions.modelAnswer: It is the stretch of road consumed while the braking force acts on the vehicle, measured in metres.

questions.stem: Define reaction time and quote its average value.
questions.modelAnswer: Reaction time is the interval between seeing a hazard and reacting to it; the human average is about 0.25 s.

questions.stem: Explain why a driver's thinking distance grows with speed even at a fixed reaction time.
questions.modelAnswer: Thinking distance is the speed multiplied by the reaction time. With the reaction time fixed, a faster vehicle covers more ground during that same pause, so the thinking distance rises in direct proportion to the speed.

questions.stem: At 20 m/s a vehicle stops in a total of 40 m, having covered 14 m during the driver's reaction. Calculate the braking distance.
questions.modelAnswer: Braking distance = stopping distance − thinking distance = 40 − 14 = 26 m.

questions.stem: Which factor list affects vehicle stopping distance?

options.text: Speed, mass, road condition, reaction time
options.explanation: The four of record.
Colour is irrelevant.
Speed and road condition belong too.

options.text: Engine size, tyre brand, music volume
options.explanation: None of those is on the list of record.

questions.stem: For a fixed braking force, increasing the vehicle's speed makes the stopping distance:

options.text: Shorter, because less stopping is needed
options.explanation: Faster travel means more stopping to do.

options.text: Unchanged, since the brakes are the same
options.explanation: The brakes being unchanged does not freeze the distance.
The greater the speed, the larger the stopping distance.
No speed yields a free stop.

questions.stem: A fully laden lorry needs a longer stop than the same lorry empty, at the same speed, chiefly because:

options.text: Its driver reacts more slowly when loaded
options.explanation: Loading does not touch the driver's reaction.

options.text: The greater mass travels further while stopping
options.explanation: Mass is a listed factor: more massive, more distance.

options.text: The road becomes icier under load
options.explanation: Loading does not change the weather.
Nonsense; the brakes remain.

questions.stem: Which change stretches the braking distance rather than the thinking distance?

options.explanation: That feeds the reaction leg.
Grip loss feeds the braking leg.
That feeds the reaction leg.
Reaction again.

questions.stem: The table shows 20 mph stopping at 12 m and 60 mph at 73 m. The comparison proves that stopping distance grows:

options.text: In fixed steps of 12 m per 20 mph
options.explanation: The steps widen: 23, 36, 53, 73.
The table contradicts that outright.

options.text: Steeper than proportionally with speed — over sixfold for a threefold speed rise
options.explanation: 60/20 is a threefold speed rise; 73/12 is a sixfold distance rise.
Sixfold for threefold is not exact proportion.

questions.stem: List the four factors of record for vehicle stopping distance.
questions.modelAnswer: Vehicle speed, vehicle mass, road condition and driver reaction time.

questions.stem: State what happens to the braking distance when speed increases at a fixed braking force.
questions.modelAnswer: It increases: the greater the speed, the greater the stopping distance.

questions.stem: Explain why icy roads lengthen a vehicle's stopping distance.
questions.modelAnswer: Ice reduces the grip between tyres and road, so the brakes work less effectively. With the braking force less effective, the vehicle travels further while coming to a stop — the braking distance stretches.

questions.stem: A lorry's thinking distance is 15 m and its braking distance is 38 m. Calculate its stopping distance.
